text: Lesson 1's meeting produces findings, but a meeting's findings live only in people's memory unless something durable captures them. That's the after-action report — a written document that turns a discussion into a record the organization can act on, reference months later, and hold itself accountable to. A real AAR isn't a narrative essay. It's a structured document with the same core sections every time.

The incident timeline is a chronological record of what happened, stated in one consistent timezone: first indicator, detection time, escalation, each containment action, and recovery completion. Root cause goes beyond the symptom that triggered the alert to the actual underlying reason — a phished credential, an unpatched vulnerability, a misconfigured firewall rule. Impact documents what was actually affected: systems, data, downtime, cost, and whether the incident needs to be reported.

Response actions taken lists the concrete steps the team executed during Detection and Analysis and Containment, Eradication and Recovery, stated plainly enough that someone who wasn't there can follow what happened. What worked and what didn't carries the lessons learned meeting's findings into the permanent record. And action items is the section that actually changes anything going forward.

The single most common way an AAR fails is an action-item list with no owner and no date. "Improve logging" is not an action item — it's a wish nobody is on the hook for. A real action item names a specific person or team, a specific deadline, and a specific, checkable outcome, like configuring a particular API access by a particular date.

Following up on Lesson 1's business email compromise, the action items read: Jordan, on the Platform team, grants the on-call IR analyst read access to MFA status, due in two weeks. Priya, the SOC lead, adds a step to the playbook requiring MFA status be checked within the first five minutes of any account-compromise incident, due in one week.

Both items get tracked the same way any other work gets tracked — in a ticketing system, with an owner and a due date — so Lesson 4's measurement step can later confirm whether they actually got done. Next up: turning a root cause like this one into a detection that catches the same pattern automatically, back in Sentinel.
